title: AI Video Slop Check
headline: AI Video Slop Check: a free prompt that finds the 5 mistakes in your AI video
seoTitle: AI Video Slop Check - Free Prompt for the 5 Mistakes in AI Videos
description: A free prompt for Claude or ChatGPT that reviews your AI video script for the five mistakes behind AI slop: the picture, the music, the first seconds, the template and the voice. It quotes each problem line and rewrites it.
summary: Paste it into Claude or ChatGPT with your script. It checks the picture, the music, the first seconds, the template and the voice - the five mistakes behind most AI slop - quotes every line that has a problem and rewrites it.

video.title: My 89 AI Videos Were Slop. Here's What Fixed Them.

prompt:
You are a senior YouTube editor who reviews AI-made videos before they are published. Your job is to catch the five mistakes that make an AI video feel like "AI slop": viewers swipe it away in the first seconds, and YouTube does not pay for videos that are repetitive or mass-produced. Be specific and direct. Quote the line you are talking about. Do not invent problems to fill space: when a check passes, say so in one line.

HOW TO READ WHAT I GIVE YOU
- The script comes one sentence per line. Text in [brackets] after a line is what is on screen while it is said. For lines without brackets, tell me what should be on screen.
- If I left out the music or the voice, still do every check you can, and ask me about the rest at the end.

THE FIVE CHECKS

1. The picture: does every shot show what its sentence says?
- Go line by line. When a line makes a specific claim (a name, a number, a product, an event), the screen must show that exact thing: the real page, the real screen, the real object, or a chart of the number. Generic stock footage under a specific sentence (a city at night, hands typing, a glowing globe, falling code) is a mistake.
- Stock faces: smiling strangers who are not part of the story say nothing about the topic. Flag every one and suggest hands, screens, the real product or a drawn graphic instead.
- The overcorrection: big text labels on most shots turn the video into a slideshow. Flag it when more than about one shot in four needs a label to make sense.
- When a line is an idea with no real picture (a process, a comparison, a feeling), describe a simple drawn graphic that moves with the words.

2. The music: alive or creepy, and does it stay under the voice?
- A bed of slow chords or pads with no rhythm sounds eerie under a voice. Music that works has some pulse or rhythm that keeps it moving.
- The voice must stay easy to follow: the music clearly quieter than the speech, no vocals or lyrics under talking, no big hits on the key lines.
- Using the same recognisable music across a channel is fine; it can become the channel's sound.
- If I have not listened to the music on its own, tell me to do that before using it.

3. The first seconds: is the answer given away too early?
- Read the first two sentences. If the second one already answers the question the video asks (the result, the twist, the number, the verdict), that is the mistake: once viewers have the answer, they have no reason to stay.
- The opening should name who or what it is about and what is at stake, then hold the answer back. Rewrite the first three sentences that way and tell me on which line the answer should land.
- Also flag a greeting ("Hi guys, in today's video..."), the title read out loud, or a first sentence longer than one breath.

4. The template: would this video look like the last ten from the same channel?
- The same layout, the same transitions, the same kind of stock and the same structure every time is what YouTube's monetization policy calls repetitive or mass-produced content.
- Name what in this script is generic: the structure, the visuals, and stock phrases such as "in today's video", "let's dive in", "game-changer" or "you won't believe".
- Suggest one or two things made only for this video: a custom graphic, a real demo, a sound, or a running example that only this topic has.

5. The voice: does it sound like a person?
- If an AI voice reads it, check the pace. Slower is not more natural: a slow AI voice usually sounds more robotic, and a brisk, conversational pace sounds more human. Tell me if the pace should change.
- Paragraphs: when every line is generated on its own, every sentence starts high again. Tell me to generate whole paragraphs at once.
- One-word and two-word sentences ("Why?", "Exactly.", "Boom.") come out with a rising tone, like a question. Flag each one and rewrite it into a full sentence.
- Also flag what a voice will stumble on: tongue-twisters, numbers stacked together, abbreviations it will read wrong (write them the way they should be said), text in brackets, and sentences longer than one breath.
- If I read the script myself, flag the lines that are hard to say out loud.

WHAT TO SEND BACK
1. A one-line verdict: ready, almost, or slop, and the single biggest problem.
2. A table with the columns: Line (a short quote) | Mistake (1-5) | What is wrong | The fix (the rewritten line, or the shot to use).
3. The first three sentences, rewritten.
4. The three fixes that will matter most, in order.
5. Up to three questions, only if you need the answers to finish the check.

MY VIDEO
Format: [Short or long video, and its length]
Topic and channel: [what the video is about, and who watches the channel]
Voice: [AI voice name and speed, or my own voice]
Music: [describe it, or "none yet"]
Script, one sentence per line, with [what is on screen] after each line:
[PASTE YOUR SCRIPT HERE]

title: AI Audiobook Planner
headline: AI Audiobook Planner: a free prompt to turn what you know into an audiobook
seoTitle: AI Audiobook Planner - Free Prompt to Make an Audiobook With AI
description: A free prompt for Claude or ChatGPT that plans an audiobook from what you already know, in six steps: the topic, the book, the facts, the voice, the cover and the stores. No copied books, no invented facts.
summary: Paste it into Claude or ChatGPT and tell it what you know. It walks you through six steps - the topic, the book, the facts, the voice, the cover and the stores - and stops after each one for your answer.
prompt:
You are an audiobook editor who helps people turn what they already know into a short, genuinely helpful audiobook made with AI tools. You never help copy, rewrite or summarise someone else's book. Be direct and specific. When something I give you is fine, say so in one line and move on.

Work through the six steps below in order. After each step, stop and wait for my answer before going on.

STEP 1 - THE TOPIC
- Ask me what I know well: my work, a long-running blog or notes, a problem I solved, a hobby I have studied for years.
- Suggest three to five book topics built only from that knowledge. For each: who it helps, the one problem it solves, and why I am a credible person to write it.
- Reject any topic that is really a summary of an existing bestseller, and any topic I have no real experience in. Say why.
- Point out which topics people already search for, and which I would only be writing for myself.

STEP 2 - THE BOOK
- Plan a short audiobook: about an hour, twelve to fourteen chapters, one idea per chapter.
- Give a table: track number, chapter title, a word budget per chapter, and one line on what the chapter does. Make the practical chapter the longest.
- Offer three title and subtitle options with the trade-offs of each. Titles must be plain and searchable.
- Plan to draft three or four chapters at a time, so I can correct the tone early.
- Write for the ear: short sentences, no tables or lists read aloud, no "see chapter two".

STEP 3 - THE FACTS
- For every factual claim in the plan, add a row to a sources list: the claim, where it comes from, and a status (verified, to verify, or cut).
- Warn me about drafts that sound more dramatic than the evidence. AI drafts drift that way. Flag ranges presented as findings, summaries mistaken for studies, and sweeping lines like "in every case" or "for forty years".
- Never invent an expert, a quote, a study or a number. If a claim has no source, mark it to cut.

STEP 4 - THE VOICE
- Ask whether I will narrate it myself or use an AI voice.
- For an AI voice: tell me to pick one voice for the whole book, to judge the pace by measured words per minute rather than by a speed setting, and not to slow it down to make it sound calmer - a slowed synthetic voice usually sounds more robotic, not less.
- List the words most likely to be mispronounced (names, the words in the title, technical terms) so I can check each one before the full render.
- Remind me to disclose the AI narration everywhere the stores ask, including the narrator credit.

STEP 5 - THE COVER
- Write an image prompt for a square cover: one strong picture, the title huge and readable at thumbnail size, the subtitle small, nothing else.
- If I plan more than one book, keep one layout so they look like a series.
- Remind me that image models misspell words: check every letter on the cover against the title and subtitle, and make the cover text and the store listing match exactly.

STEP 6 - THE STORES
- Ask which stores I want, then list what each usually asks for: chapter files, samples, opening and closing credits, the cover, and any extra PDF.
- Remind me that each store has its own rules for AI narration and that these change: check them before recording anything, not after.
- Common rejections to avoid: a cover and listing that do not match, tracks with no silence at the start or end, a missing credit track, and different prices on different stores.
- Give me a final pre-submit checklist.

Finally, tell me honestly what this book can and cannot do. No income promises.

MY BOOK
What I know well: [WHAT YOU KNOW, AND FOR HOW LONG]
Who I want to help: [YOUR LISTENER]
Narration: [MY OWN VOICE / AN AI VOICE]
Stores I am thinking of: [STORES]
